name: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
title: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
answer: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to sort large document collections by relevance, most often in litigation, investigations and regulatory responses. The scope runs from simple keyword and rule-based filters through supervised learning on reviewer decisions to more recent approaches that combine sampling, active learning and large language models. It sits inside e-discovery, where the practical question is not whether a model can rank documents but whether the ranking can be defended to a court, an opponent or a regulator. Related work includes privilege review, redaction, deduplication and the production of documents in a reviewable format.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on document review platforms that ingest files from email, shared drives, chat and case management systems, extract text and metadata, and index everything for search and ranking. These platforms typically combine a database or search engine, a machine learning service for classification and clustering, and a user interface where reviewers code documents and see model scores. Processing pipelines handle optical character recognition, language detection, near-duplicate detection and threading of email conversations. Storage and compute are usually cloud-hosted, with access controls, audit logs and export tooling for productions.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical matter starts with a seed set of documents coded by senior reviewers, which trains a classifier to rank the remaining population. Teams then iterate: review the highest-ranked documents, correct the model, and sample the lower-ranked and excluded regions to estimate how much relevant material is being missed. Statistical sampling and recall estimates are used to decide when the ranking is good enough to stop, and the process is documented so that the method can be explained later. Modern variants add active learning, where the model selects the next documents for review, and transformer-based models that can be prompted rather than trained from scratch. Quality control includes reviewer consistency checks, blinded samples and comparison against keyword searches.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Courts and regulators increasingly expect the parties to explain how a predictive coding workflow was designed, validated and monitored, not just that it was used. That means keeping records of seed sets, training rounds, sampling plans, recall estimates and the reasoning behind cutoffs, plus a way to show that privileged or protected material was handled correctly. Proportionality, defensibility and transparency are the recurring standards, and the burden usually falls on the party proposing the method to show it is reasonable. Data protection rules add constraints on where documents are stored, who can see them and how long they are kept, and cross-border matters can require local review or transfer safeguards. None of this is legal advice, and the specific obligations depend on the jurisdiction and the matter.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration of review platforms with generative models, so that classification, summarisation and privilege flagging happen in one workflow rather than several. Expect more emphasis on validation and explainability, because a model that cannot be described is hard to defend, and on continuous active learning that keeps improving as review proceeds. Smaller matters may benefit most, since the cost of setting up a supervised workflow has fallen and prompt-based methods need less labelled data. The open questions are how to audit model behaviour over time, how to handle multilingual and multimodal material, and how to keep human review meaningful when the model is doing most of the ranking.
